title: Zero-copy blob parameter transfer via TransferableTypedData
impact: A large `Uint8List` blob write param crosses the main->writer isolate hop via `SendPort.send`'s object-graph copy, which lands the payload on the shared GC heap. Exp 234 wraps blob params `>= 256 KB` in `TransferableTypedData` — one plain memcpy into malloc'd external memory, then a constant-time ownership move and a zero-copy `materialize()` view on the writer; smaller blobs and non-blob params take the unchanged direct path (the fast path returns the input list with no allocation). Answers the direction's open question — for **256 KB-512 KB single-row blob INSERTs the hop cost is a material fraction of the write, and the wrapped route is a reproduced ~15-20% end-to-end speedup** (256 KB -16.4% / -22.7%, 512 KB -10.4% / -11.8% across order-flipped passes; every 256/512 KB leg candidate-faster across ~7 passes while sub-threshold 64/128 KB controls flip sign as noise). Mechanism attribution (per-call table + per-lane `--verbose_gc` on the real path) shows both routes copy the payload exactly once on main — the win is the copy's *destination*: direct sends make every in-flight blob live GC-heap data (29 GCs / 8.6 ms pause vs 20 GCs / 1.2 ms per 300 x 256 KB inserts), and each collection safepoints the isolate group including the writer mid-step. The 256 KB floor is measured: transport is +22.7% *slower* at 64 KB (wrap bookkeeping vs the graph copy's near-free fast path) and neutral at >= 1 MB (WAL write dominates; huge payloads skip new space). Sharpens exp 005 rather than contradicting it: a raw blob has no structure to encode, so only destination and machinery costs remain. Internal knob (not public API); adds a large-blob round-trip correctness test.
